bodyMarkdown:
## Before you start

Distance = speed x time, and comfort converting between km/h and m/s.

## The idea in plain language

Sit in a moving train and look out of the window. A train coming the other way flashes past in a second. A train going the same way as you, at almost your speed, seems to crawl alongside for ages.

Neither train changed speed. What changed is the speed **relative to you**. Coming towards you, the speeds add. Going the same way, they subtract.

## What is actually going on

Relative speed lets you pretend one object is standing still. Instead of tracking two moving things, you freeze one and give the other the combined speed. The distance between them then closes at that single rate, and the problem becomes an ordinary distance-equals-speed-times-time question.

Opposite directions: add the speeds. Same direction: subtract them. That is the entire idea, and it powers trains, boats, races and circular tracks too.

## Every question type you will meet

Each of these is a shape a question in this topic actually comes in. Learn to recognise the shape first — in a timed paper, picking the right method is most of the battle, and the arithmetic is the easy part.

### 1. Approaching from opposite ends

**Spot it when:** two objects starting apart and moving towards each other.

1. Add the speeds to get the closing speed.
2. Divide the initial gap by that closing speed.

**Worked through:** A 300 km gap closing at $60 + 40 = 100$ km/h takes 3 hours.

### 2. Catching up

**Spot it when:** one object chasing another in the same direction, often starting later.

1. Subtract the speeds to get the closing speed.
2. Find the head start in distance: the leader's speed times its head-start time.
3. Divide that distance by the closing speed.

**Worked through:** A car at 80 chasing one at 60 that left an hour earlier closes a 60 km gap at 20 km/h, taking 3 hours.

### 3. Average speed over a there-and-back journey

**Spot it when:** the same distance covered twice at different speeds.

1. Never average the two speeds.
2. Use total distance over total time, or the harmonic mean $\dfrac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2}$ for two equal legs.
3. Check the answer is below the plain average — it always is.

**Worked through:** 4 km/h out and 6 km/h back averages $\dfrac{2 \times 24}{10} = 4.8$ km/h.

### 4. Late and early arrivals

**Spot it when:** 'at 5 km/h he is 10 minutes late, at 6 km/h he is 5 minutes early'.

1. The distance is the same both times, so write it as speed times time for each case.
2. Express both times relative to the on-time duration $t$, converting minutes to hours.
3. Set the two distances equal and solve for $t$.

**Worked through:** $5\left(t + \dfrac{1}{6}\right) = 6\left(t - \dfrac{1}{12}\right)$ gives $t = \dfrac{4}{3}$ hours and a distance of 7.5 km.

## Check yourself

You are ready to start practising this topic when you can:

- Decide instantly whether speeds add or subtract.
- Turn a head start in time into a head start in distance.
- Compute an average speed correctly for equal distances and explain why it is not the mean.
- Set up a late-and-early question using the fact that the distance is unchanged.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: Two cars 300 km apart drive towards each other at 60 km/h and 40 km/h. When do they meet?
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
They approach each other at $60 + 40 = 100$ km/h.

The 300 km gap closes at 100 km/h, so they meet after $\dfrac{300}{100} = 3$ hours.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: Freeze one car and let the other drive at 100 km/h — the meeting time is unchanged.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: A man walks to school at 4 km/h and returns along the same road at 6 km/h. What is his average speed?
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
Average speed is total distance over total time, never the average of the two speeds.

Take the one-way distance as 12 km (any number works). Going takes $\dfrac{12}{4} = 3$ hours; returning takes $\dfrac{12}{6} = 2$ hours. Total: 24 km in 5 hours.

Average speed $= \dfrac{24}{5} = 4.8$ km/h.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: For two equal distances use the harmonic mean: $\dfrac{2 \times 4 \times 6}{4 + 6} = 4.8$. Note it is below 5, the naive average — you spend longer at the slower speed, so the slow leg counts for more.

formulaCards.title: Relative speed
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Towards each other: $v_1 + v_2$. Same direction: $|v_1 - v_2|$.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: At 70 and 50 km/h: closing at 120 km/h head-on, or 20 km/h if one chases the other.

formulaCards.title: Average speed over two equal distances
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: 60 km/h out and 40 km/h back gives $\dfrac{2 \times 60 \times 40}{100} = 48$ km/h.

formulaCards.title: Unit conversion
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Multiply by $\dfrac{5}{18}$ to turn km/h into m/s, and by $\dfrac{18}{5}$ to go back.

commonTraps: Taking the plain average of two speeds. That is only right if the two legs took equal time, not equal distance.
Mixing km/h and m/s in the same calculation without converting.
Adding speeds when the objects move the same way, or subtracting when they move towards each other.
